White-naped honeyeater (Melithreptus lunatus) eggs, when incubated at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], typically hatch after 12 days [ab = 12 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with the incubation durations observed in other medium-sized meliphagids. The newly emerged hatchlings are remarkably altricial, with a mass of only 1.9 grams [Ww0 = 1.9 grams] at the moment of first feeding, representing an initial wet weight that constitutes a very small fraction of the adult body mass. This modest neonatal mass underscores the substantial parental investment required during the nestling phase, during which the chick undergoes rapid somatic growth. The relatively short incubation period, combined with a low hatchling mass, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes a high intrinsic rate of increase, which may be linked to the species' occupation of climatically unpredictable forest edges and dry sclerophyll woodlands.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the rest of the species' ontogenetic trajectory unfolds in a predictable fashion. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], a remarkably early age for a passerine of this body size that likely reflects a selective pressure for rapid turnover in a seasonally variable environment at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Subsequently, the fledgling period, culminating in the achievement of sustained flight and nutritional independence from the provisioning adult, is completed at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching], which falls squarely within the 14 to 16.5 day range reported for other congeners at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The first successful brood is initiated at 1.1 years after hatching [tR = 1.1 years after hatching], indicating a delay between physiological maturity and the commencement of actual reproductive activity, likely driven by constraints related to territory acquisition and the establishment of a stable foraging niche at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

A comprehensive understanding of the species' physiology requires examining its metabolic demands, which have been investigated through controlled respirometry. Under standard basal conditions at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting metabolic rate of adult White-naped honeyeaters was measured at 45 milliliters per hour [JOi = 45 milliliters per hour]. This value, expressed as the maximum basal metabolic rate for the species, is consistent with the relatively high metabolic demands of small-bodied passerines that maintain an insectivorous-nectarivorous diet. The energetic costs associated with sustaining such a metabolic rate are significant, particularly during the breeding season when adults must simultaneously provision nestlings and defend territories. The baseline oxygen consumption recorded at this temperature provides a crucial reference point for understanding how the species budgets its energy intake across different life-history stages, particularly when compared to the lower metabolic rates observed in the larger honeyeaters of the genus Anthochaera.

The reproductive output of Melithreptus lunatus is characterized by a modest clutch size and a low annual frequency. Breeding females typically lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch attempted each year [F_R_i = single clutch attempted each year]. This combination of a small clutch and a single annual nesting attempt results in a constrained annual reproductive output that is typical of many honeyeaters occupying stable but resource-poor environments. The low fecundity is compensated by a relatively high adult survival rate, as reflected in the species' lifespan. At the standard metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the oldest documented individual in a long-term field study survived for 12.3 years [am = 12.3 years], a longevity that is notable for a passerine of only 13 to 15 grams, placing it among the more long-lived members of the Meliphagidae family.

Significant sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is evident in this honeyeater. Adult females attain a maximum stable body mass of 13.4 grams [Wwi = 13.4 grams], whereas adult males are consistently larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams]. This approximately 12% difference in asymptotic mass is a common pattern among Australian honeyeaters and is thought to be linked to intrasexual competition among males for access to nectar-rich territories and breeding females. The larger body size in males likely confers advantages in aggressive encounters, but it also imposes higher absolute metabolic costs. The divergence in adult mass between the sexes is already apparent by the late nestling stage and is fully established by the time of fledging, underscoring the role of differential parental provisioning or sex-specific growth trajectories during the critical developmental window.
